questions.stem: The longest river in India is the:

options.option_text: Brahmaputra
Ganga
Godavari
Narmada

questions.explanation: The Ganga — ~2,525 km — is the longest river flowing mainly within India. The Brahmaputra is longer overall (~2,900 km) but most of its length is in Tibet and Bangladesh. The Godavari (~1,465 km) is the longest river of peninsular India and is called the 'Dakshin Ganga'. Narmada (~1,312 km) flows westwards into the Arabian Sea through a rift valley.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Ganga river originates as the 'Bhagirathi' from a glacier called:

options.option_text: Milam glacier
Gangotri glacier
Pindari glacier
Siachen glacier

questions.explanation: The Bhagirathi emerges from the Gangotri glacier at Gaumukh, Uttarakhand (~4,100 m). It joins the Alaknanda at Devprayag to form the Ganga. The other 'prayags' (confluences on the upper Ganga): Vishnuprayag, Nandprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag, Devprayag ('panch prayag'). Siachen is the source of the Nubra river (a Shyok tributary of the Indus).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which of the following rivers flows through a rift valley?

options.option_text: Ganga
Narmada
Godavari
Krishna

questions.explanation: The Narmada (and the Tapi) flow through rift valleys — linear depressions between parallel mountain ranges (Vindhya to the north, Satpura to the south). They flow westwards into the Arabian Sea — exceptions among the mostly east-flowing peninsular rivers. Most rivers of the peninsula (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi) flow east into the Bay of Bengal and form deltas.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Match the river with its source. A. Indus. B. Yamuna. C. Kaveri. D. Mahanadi. List-II: 1. Lake Manasarovar area (Tibet), 2. Yamunotri, 3. Talakaveri (Brahmagiri), 4. Sihawa hills (Chhattisgarh).
questions.explanation: Indus — rises near Lake Manasarovar in Tibet. Yamuna — from Yamunotri in the Himalayas (Uttarakhand). Kaveri — from Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri hills (Kodagu district, Karnataka). Mahanadi — from the Sihawa hills in Chhattisgarh. Other peninsular sources — Godavari (Triambakeshwar, MH), Krishna (Mahabaleshwar, MH), Narmada (Amarkantak, MP).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The Brahmaputra river enters India from Arunachal Pradesh, where it is locally called:

options.option_text: Tsangpo
Siang (or Dihang)
Jamuna
Padma

questions.explanation: The Brahmaputra system — in Tibet called Tsangpo; enters India as the Siang / Dihang in Arunachal Pradesh; becomes the Brahmaputra in Assam after joining the Lohit and Dibang near Sadiya; in Bangladesh called Jamuna (not to be confused with Yamuna of the Ganga basin); joins the Padma (Ganga's name in Bangladesh) and the Meghna before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The largest tributary of the Ganga (by catchment area) is the:

options.option_text: Yamuna
Gandak
Kosi
Son

questions.explanation: The Yamuna — rising from Yamunotri — is the largest tributary of the Ganga by both length (~1,375 km) and catchment area. It joins the Ganga at Prayagraj (Allahabad) in the 'Triveni Sangam' (with the mythological Saraswati). Other major Ganga tributaries — Ramganga, Ghaghara, Gandak, Kosi (from the Himalayan north), and Chambal, Betwa, Son (from the Vindhya/Satpura south).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: The river sacred to the Sikhs as the 'River of the Punjab', flowing past Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) — via Amritsar, is the:

options.option_text: Sutlej
Ravi
Beas
Chenab

questions.explanation: The Ravi flows near Amritsar; the sarovar of the Golden Temple is fed by it (and by groundwater). The five rivers of the Punjab — Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej — give the region its name ('panj' = five + 'aab' = water). All five are tributaries of the Indus. Under the Indus Waters Treaty (1960), Pakistan gets full use of the three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) and India of the three eastern (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej).
questions.subject: Geography

questions.stem: Which river is popularly called 'Dakshin Ganga' owing to its immense religious sanctity and the large number of pilgrimage centres along its course?

options.option_text: Krishna river, draining parts of the southern Deccan
Godavari river, the longest peninsular river in India
Kaveri river, originating in Brahmagiri Hills of Coorg
Mahanadi river, flowing through Chhattisgarh and Odisha

questions.explanation: Godavari is called 'Dakshin Ganga' because of its great religious sanctity and numerous pilgrimage sites — Nashik, Paithan, Rajahmundry — along its ~1,465 km course, making it the longest peninsular river. Kaveri is sometimes locally called 'Dakshin Ganga' in Karnataka, but the well-established, widely accepted title belongs to Godavari. Krishna and Mahanadi do not carry this epithet.

questions.stem: The Narmada (flowing westward to the Arabian Sea) and the Son river (flowing eastward to join the Ganga) share a common highland origin. Which plateau is this?

options.option_text: Chota Nagpur Plateau in the eastern part of Jharkhand
Malwa Plateau in the north-western region of Madhya Pradesh
Amarkantak Plateau in the eastern part of Madhya Pradesh
Deccan Plateau on the leeward side of the Western Ghats

questions.explanation: The Amarkantak highlands in eastern Madhya Pradesh (Anuppur district) are the source of both Narmada and Son — a classic PYQ-tested fact. The rivers flow in opposite directions from virtually the same watershed: Narmada heads west through a rift valley to the Arabian Sea, while Son heads northeast to join the Ganga at Patna. The Malwa Plateau is a common distractor because the Narmada flows along its southern edge, but the actual source is Amarkantak.

questions.stem: Historically dubbed the 'Sorrow of Bengal' for its devastating seasonal floods, the Damodar river traverses which pair of states before joining the Hooghly?

options.option_text: Bihar and West Bengal, joining the Ganga near Patna city
Jharkhand and West Bengal, emptying into the Hooghly River
Chhattisgarh and Odisha, draining directly into the Bay of Bengal
Odisha and West Bengal, merging with the Ganga at Farakka

questions.explanation: The Damodar originates in the Chota Nagpur Plateau (Jharkhand) and flows eastward through West Bengal before joining the Hooghly near Hugli-Chinsurah. The Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) was set up in 1948 to control its floods. Bihar is the most tempting wrong choice because Jharkhand was carved out of Bihar in 2000 — older references associate the Damodar with Bihar. Chhattisgarh and Odisha are entirely unrelated to its course.

questions.stem: The Mahi is one of the few Indian rivers that crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice during its westward journey. Into which water body does the Mahi eventually drain?

options.option_text: Gulf of Mannar off the southeastern coast of Tamil Nadu
Arabian Sea off the Konkan coast of Maharashtra state
Gulf of Khambhat along the central Gujarat coastline
Rann of Kutch, the seasonal salt marsh in northern Gujarat

questions.explanation: The Mahi rises in Madhya Pradesh, briefly enters Rajasthan, then flows through Gujarat to drain into the Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay). Its looping course causes it to cross the Tropic of Cancer twice — a widely tested geographic oddity. The Rann of Kutch distractor is tempting because it is also in Gujarat, but the Luni is the river that drains toward the Rann. The Konkan coast and Gulf of Mannar are in entirely different drainage regions.

questions.stem: India's first approved river-interlinking project under the National Perspective Plan connects the Ken and Betwa — both right-bank tributaries of which major river?

options.option_text: Ganga, flowing through the alluvial plains of Uttar Pradesh
Chambal, cutting through the ravines of the Malwa Plateau
Yamuna, running from the Himalayas down to Prayagraj
Narmada, traversing the rift valley of central India

questions.explanation: Both Ken (joining Yamuna near Banda, UP) and Betwa (joining Yamuna near Hamirpur, UP) are right-bank tributaries of the Yamuna. The Ken-Betwa Link Project transfers surplus water from the Ken (Madhya Pradesh) to the water-scarce Betwa basin. Chambal is the most tempting distractor because it drains the same Bundelkhand-Malwa region — but Chambal itself is a tributary of Yamuna, not the parent of Ken or Betwa.

questions.stem: Under the Indus Waters Treaty signed between India and Pakistan in 1960, which three rivers were designated 'western rivers' and allocated to Pakistan for unrestricted use?

options.option_text: Sutlej, Beas, and Ravi — allocated exclusively to India
Indus main stem, Jhelum, and Chenab — the western rivers
Ravi, Chenab, and Jhelum — India retains storage rights only
Jhelum, Beas, and Chenab — under shared seasonal protocols

questions.explanation: The IWT divides the six Indus-system rivers into eastern (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej — to India) and western (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab — to Pakistan). Option A describes India's eastern rivers, the most common reversal error in exams. Option C incorrectly includes Ravi (an eastern river) alongside Jhelum and Chenab. Option D incorrectly substitutes Beas (eastern, India's) for the Indus main stem. India retains limited rights over western rivers for storage and run-of-river hydropower but cannot divert their flow substantially.

questions.stem: The Barak river drains southern Assam's Barak Valley and crosses into Bangladesh, where it bifurcates at Amalshid. What are the two channels formed at this bifurcation?

options.option_text: Surma and Kushiyara — forming the upper Meghna river system
Padma and Jamuna — the main distributaries of the Ganga
Brahmaputra and Buri Ganga — converging near Dhaka city
Teesta and Atrai — draining the northwestern Bengal plains

questions.explanation: At Amalshid on the India-Bangladesh border, the Barak splits into the Surma (flowing northwest) and Kushiyara (flowing south). Both channels eventually reconverge and feed into the Meghna — making the Barak the upstream source of Bangladesh's largest estuary river. This tests whether candidates know northeast India's separate Barak-Meghna drainage system. Options B, C, and D name rivers from entirely unrelated drainage systems: the Ganga-Padma, the Brahmaputra, and the Teesta-Atrai basins respectively.
